big_case_rationale: A recurring military-divorce question (roughly a quarter of two million military retirees waive retired pay for disability pay, and settlement indemnity clauses are standard drafting), with an entrenched state-high-court split; consequential for family-law practice and veterans' former spouses, but a technical preemption question of little general public salience.

semantic_claims.proposition: The majority will hold that the USFSPA (10 U.S.C. 1408), as construed in Mansell and Howell, restricts only what a state court may itself treat and divide as marital property, and does not preempt enforcement of a veteran's voluntary, bargained-for promise in a divorce settlement to indemnify a former spouse for retired pay later waived or converted to disability-based pay. It will distinguish Howell as a court-imposed restoration of a divided asset rather than enforcement of a contract, confine Mansell to the state court's own power of division, and rest on the presumption that a statutory protection is waivable by the party it protects (the Mezzanatto line) together with Rose v. Rose's recognition that a veteran's personal obligations may be enforced against him notwithstanding the character of the funds, while declining to treat 38 U.S.C. 5301's anti-assignment clause as reaching an indemnity obligation payable from any source.

The majority's stated ground will be a categorical rule for negotiated indemnification and waiver provisions in divorce settlements generally, not confined to this decree's wording, to Chapter 61 disability-retirement pay, or to pre-Howell agreements; but it will stop short of deciding whether this particular 2016 decree and post-judgment order in fact embody such an agreement or what remedy follows, leaving those state-law questions (including the Rule 60(b) and spousal-support framing the trial court used) to the North Dakota courts on remand.
